#8270. COLD RELIC: A Case Study in Impersonation and Compromise

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2685 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

COLD RELIC: A Case Study in Impersonation and Compromise

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Visibility and context on the threats that matter most.
  • Written by: Josh Murchie, John Wolfram, Joseph Spero, Peter Ukhanov, Fernando Tomlinson, Jr., Wesley Shields.
  • According to recent reports, over the past year, Mandiant has responded to a series of linked intrusions demonstrating how Russian cyber espionage group COLD RELIC (formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057; also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) turns a single cloud compromise into a springboard for ongoing third party compromise and espionage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Visibility and context on the threats that matter most.

Written by: Josh Murchie, John Wolfram, Joseph Spero, Peter Ukhanov, Fernando Tomlinson, Jr., Wesley Shields.

According to recent reports, over the past year, Mandiant has responded to a series of linked intrusions demonstrating how Russian cyber espionage group COLD RELIC (formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057; also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) turns a single cloud compromise into a springboard for ongoing third party compromise and espionage. Most recently, Mandiant investigated a 2026 compromise at a US-based organization where COLD RELIC directly weaponized data, the corporate staff directory, and identities stolen during a late-2025 compromise, which Mandiant also investigated, at a separate US-based organization.

It has been revealed that COLD RELIC is a Russian state-sponsored threat group that the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has assessed operates within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). The group is known for implementing sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns with the aim to gain access to information of strategic or political relevance to the Russian government, as well as to leverage compromised access to target compromised individuals’ broader social and professional networks. Once COLD RELIC compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets. While COLD RELIC has largely maintained a low profile, yielding minimal public reporting relative to other Russia-nexus threat actors, it has been highly successful at compromising high-value targets (including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America) while maintaining a consistent operational tempo.

While Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has tracked and disrupted COLD RELIC phishing campaigns since 2015, recent Mandiant incident response investigations have uncovered critical new insights into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft. We are sharing this end-to-end analysis—along with actionable detection and hardening guidance—to help organizations defend against COLD RELIC’s ongoing use of stolen pretexts, localized residential proxies, and cross-cloud identity abuse. As part of our efforts to thwart this threat actor, we problem Government-backed attack alerts when we detect COLD RELIC targeting Google accounts. COLD RELIC remains an active threat; GTIG has observed evidence of new phishing operations as recently as November 2026.

Industry observers note that over more than a decade of tracking COLD RELIC alongside Mandiant incident response investigations, we have observed the group continually refine how it leverages data harvested from one intrusion to enable follow-on operations against downstream targets. In late 2025, COLD RELIC downloaded a large volume of data from a US-based organization, searching for names, email addresses, and email archives, likely to fulfill broader intelligence requirements. In 2026, Mandiant investigated a subsequent COLD RELIC intrusion at a second US-based organization where phishing URL parameters and impersonation pretexts indicated that COLD RELIC likely leveraged contact and relationship context from the first organization to target the second.

Sources indicate that one of the hallmarks of COLD RELIC phishing campaigns is the use of a compromised website as the initial link that will redirect the target to the actual phishing domain. This provides COLD RELIC with a layer of misdirection and hides their phishing domains, while also giving them a chance to fingerprint anyone visiting the link to determine if they should be redirected or not. A COLD RELIC phishing link usually contains a parameter on the end of it with a value that is set by the attacker and often indicates a relationship to a previous victim or what the lure is. For example, a URL might look like these (though this is not always the case):.

Figure 1: Sample URLs incorporating targeted individuals’ names or lure topics.

It has been revealed that during Mandiant’s incident response investigation at the second US-based organization, responders identified that COLD RELIC initiated contact over an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee from the first victim organization. In parallel, GTIG correlated a COLD RELIC redirector URL from the intrusion that had been submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026, whose query parameter referenced the first victim organization.

According to recent reports, during the late-2025 intrusion, GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise the cloud productivity environment of a US-based organization. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC leveraged a residential proxy network in the US located in close geographical proximity to the victim. COLD RELIC authenticated using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account, in combination with a multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notification fatigue attack. After the victim user accepted an MFA request, COLD RELIC registered a device model previously unseen within the tenant of the victim organization. COLD RELIC leveraged passkeys, MFA backup codes, and rogue MFA devices to retain access throughout the intrusion.

COLD RELIC used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization’s cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a COLD RELIC-operated email account and downloading files directly. While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, COLD RELIC accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion. COLD RELIC also exported full employee lists and initiated a domain-wide data export via Google Workspace Customer Takeout using Super Admin privileges. Unlike individual end-user Google Takeout, Customer Takeout is an administrative tenant-wide export tool; these requests are logged in Google Workspace Admin audit logs (CUSTOMER_TAKEOUT_CREATED), and administrators can also disable Google Takeout for owners at the organizational level.

Following mass data theft and antiforensics activities, COLD RELIC maintained access to the victim organization for several months and performed additional activities including:.

Email inbox sync via OAuth to external email clients.

Reauthentication using unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys that persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls.

Targeted cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information, and other documents relevant to COLD RELIC’s intelligence collection requirements.

In a recent development, when the threat actor was removed from the victim organization’s infrastructure, GTIG observed COLD RELIC leveraging email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization. These impersonated accounts were used to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles with renewed social engineering attempts.

Industry observers note that during the second intrusion, COLD RELIC demonstrated competency in navigating multi-cloud environments and federated authentication mechanisms. GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a US-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC impersonated an employee of the organization impacted in Case Study 1 to establish a pretext for communications over a secure messaging app. The threat actor ultimately shared phishing links during the course of the conversation. These phishing links, designed to steal credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID, redirected the victim to document lures relevant to the ongoing conversation in order to avoid raising suspicion. Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, COLD RELIC registered and used a fresh MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion.

A redacted and abbreviated version of the social engineering conversation is included below (image generated with LLMs):.

Figure 2: Redacted, LLM-generated depiction of observed threat actor social engineering engagement.

According to recent reports, by impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, COLD RELIC increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, COLD RELIC was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive.

After gaining initial access to an organization, COLD RELIC registers rogue MFA devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence. Once persistence is secured, COLD RELIC conducts aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations, accessing email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. While COLD RELIC's primary objective post-compromise is mass collection and download of files and email archives, it simultaneously performs targeted queries for specific terms of interest. In particular, COLD RELIC searches for credentials, personnel information, email archives (.pst files), and documents related to their collection requirements. Additionally, COLD RELIC seeks out data that can support subsequent spear-phishing operations, including organizational rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules to build convincing pretexts for future targets.

In a recent development, beyond seeking out data to support subsequent operations, COLD RELIC also appeared to repurpose the account used in Case Study 2 for follow on targeting. After the compromise, the encrypted messaging application used for the initial approach recorded that the threat actor changed their profile name to a completely latest person. GTIG believes this new persona was likely used to continue to target other organizations in the same professional circles in a similar manner to both of the cases documented here.

COLD RELIC’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners. Their ability to navigate across multiple cloud ecosystems highlights that organizations must defend their entire identity estate holistically. GTIG will continue to track, disrupt, and expose COLD RELIC infrastructure to protect global cloud owners.

As previously mentioned, GTIG has observed COLD RELIC heavily rely on residential proxy networks in the course of their intrusions. Moreover, the group goes one step further in obfuscating their activities by selecting proxies that geolocate to the same approximate location as their victim owners, thereby avoiding impossible travel or other heuristic-based alerting mechanisms. GTIG recommends enriching authentication logs with residential proxy and VPN IP reputation feeds, alerting on sudden residential ASN shifts for privileged accounts, and applying conditional access policies to block or detect logons from known proxy networks.

Industry observers note that in some cases, the severity and scope of COLD RELIC intrusions were amplified due to consumers storing credentials and other secrets within their organization’s cloud storage platforms. This enabled COLD RELIC to pivot to additional accounts or services that it would not have otherwise been able to access, including users’ personal accounts which are typically unmonitored by their employers. Organizations can implement cloud storage Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies, such as Google Workspace’s Security & Data Protection, to warn or block users attempting to create, upload, or externally share files matching sensitive patterns.

In at least one case, GTIG observed that a victim organization identified the intrusion and attempted to remediate COLD RELIC’s access to their cloud tenant via password resets for impacted accounts. However, because the threat actor hijacked sessions and the victim organization failed to also revoke all existing sessions for the accounts in question, COLD RELIC maintained access. In similar circumstances, such as Business Email Compromise (BEC) intrusions, GTIG recommends organizations revoke all user sessions in addition to forcing password resets for impacted accounts. Organizations should implement the following recommendations:.

Identity & Multi-Factor Authentication.

In a recent development, enforce Phishing-Resistant MFA (FIDO2 / WebAuthn): Replace SMS, voice, and push notifications with hardware security keys (e.g., Titan Security Keys). Hardware keys are bound to the origin URL and cannot be intercepted by AiTM reverse proxies or approved via fatigue attacks.

Restrict and Audit Passkey Registrations: Monitor identity logs for passkey registrations and rogue device enrollments, particularly on administrative accounts.

Harden MFA Registration: Require existing administrators or out-of-band identity verification to approve latest MFA devices or secondary authenticators (such as Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys).

Organizations and individuals may consider enrolling in the Advanced Protection Program.

Session Management & Incident Response.

It has been revealed that mandate Session & OAuth Revocation in BEC Playbooks: When remediating suspected account compromise, password changes alone are insufficient. Administrators must immediately revoke all active browser sessions, refresh tokens, and authorized third-party OAuth app permissions across both Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID, and remove any unauthorized passkeys, backup codes, or MFA devices.

Audit Third-Party OAuth Grants: Continuously review authorized third-party applications in Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, flagging unexpected native desktop email clients (e.g., Thunderbird) or external mail services (e.g., Proton Mail).

Network & Infrastructure Controls.

Detect & Block Residential Proxy Logons: Restrict administrative access from consumer ISPs, VPNs, and known residential proxy ASN ranges (e.g., AS5650, AS20115).

Cross-Cloud DLP Policies: Deploy Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules across cloud storage (Google Drive, OneDrive, SharePoint) to alert on documents containing sensitive terms (e.g., passwords, roster, .pst) or to restrict mass external file-sharing.

T1621: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation.

Monitor for MFA Spam: Alert on multiple failed login or MFA challenge events for a single user in a short timeframe, followed closely by a successful authentication from the same IP address.

T1114.002: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection.

T1528: Steal Application Access Token.

Unapproved OAuth Scopes: Alert on fresh OAuth authorizations (Authorize event in GWS OAuth logs) granting broad scopes (e.g., https://mail.google.com/) to non-standard or unapproved email clients like Proton or Thunderbird.

Automated Data Exfiltration Attempt.

Customer Takeout Initiation: Generate alerts for the creation of any tenant-wide collection or export (e.g., Customer Takeout Created in GWS Admin logs), as this is a technique that can result in data exfiltration of an entire tenant.

It has been revealed that anomalous Download Volume: Monitor logs for spikes in file downloads (e.g. Download events in GWS Drive logs) by a single user within a short period of time, particularly originating from non-corporate ASNs/IPs or known residential proxy networks.

Data Theft via External Sharing.

T1567.002: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage.

External File Sharing Anomalies: Monitor logs for a spike in documents being shared externally (e.g., GWS Drive User Sharing Permissions Change or Visibility changed to shared_externally), particularly to free email providers (e.g., @gmail.com).

T1098.005: Account Manipulation: Device Registration.

Fresh MFA/Device Enrollment: Alert on new passkey enrollments (e.g., GWS Passkey enrolled events) or device registrations (GWS Device Registered events), particularly when originating from unexpected geographic locations or immediately following an MFA fatigue pattern.

T1078.004: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts.

Backup Code Usage: Monitor logs for authentications with MFA backup codes (e.g., GWS User logs where the Login Challenge Type is Backup code), particularly if it originates from a non-corporate ASN or known residential proxy networks.

Impairing Defenses via Alert Deletion.

T1562.008: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Cloud Logs / Alerts.

Alert Center Tampering: Alert on any user modifying or deleting security alerts (e.g., Batch Delete Operation Performed events in GWS Admin logs), particularly if the user is deleting alerts related to their own account or critical severity alerts (e.g., GWS Government-backed attack alerts).

Internal Reconnaissance via User List.

T1087.004: Account Discovery: Cloud Account.

Industry observers note that directory Export: Alert on domain user exports (e.g., User List Download events in GWS Admin logs). While admins may do this legitimately, it should be heavily scrutinized, particularly when performed from unknown devices.

T1082: System Information Discovery.

In a recent development, admin Log Querying: Monitor logs for users performing audit log queries (e.g., Investigation Query events in GWS Admin logs). Unexpected querying of security, access, or audit logs may indicate a threat actor attempting to perform counter-forensics.

Searching for Passwords & Archives.

T1083: File and Directory Discovery.

T1552.001: Credentials In Files.

Sensitive File Search: Monitor logs for file directory keyword searches (e.g., Item search performed events in GWS Drive logs) containing terms related to archives or credentials such as .pst, .bak, password, cred, or repeated accesses/downloads of documents explicitly titled with credential-related keywords.

Google SecOps customers have access to these broad category rules and more under the Mandiant Frontline Threats rule pack. The activity discussed in the blog post is detected in Google SecOps under the rule names:.

Google Workspace Successful MFA Fatigue Attack.

Google Workspace Customer Takeout Initiated.

Google Workspace Alert Center Alert Deletion.

Google Workspace Directory User List Download.

Google Workspace Drive Bulk External or Freemail File Sharing.

Google Workspace Device or Passkey Enrollment Following MFA Fatigue.

Google Workspace OAuth Broad Mail Scope Granted to Unapproved Client.

arXiv:2611.22583v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22575v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (265 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22543v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (180 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.22541v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

#8255. JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (207 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

#8252. Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (351 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (351 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22537v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on latest intends 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.

arXiv:2611.22532v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past year, we’ve focused on making Looker easier to use for every business user.
  • The next step is elevating how your data is seen and interpreted.
  • Recent findings suggest that this November, we are rolling out a major update for Looker’s visual language that brings newly introduced native chart types and dashboard controls to your dashboards, Explores, and feeds into your generative Data Apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Over the past year, we’ve focused on making Looker easier to use for every business user. We started by redesigning the exploration experience with drag-and-drop workspaces, streamlined field pickers, and conversational analytics to make it easier to start from a blank canvas.

The next step is elevating how your data is seen and interpreted.

Recent findings suggest that this November, we are rolling out a major update for Looker’s visual language that brings newly introduced native chart types and dashboard controls to your dashboards, Explores, and feeds into your generative Data Apps. Everything runs on Looker's governed semantic foundation and context from Knowledge Catalog. Here's what's new:.

KPI visualizations: Display core metrics with explicit period-over-period delta indicators, percentage trends, and directional status at a glance.

Displaying core business metrics and period-over-period trends with a KPI visualization.

Tracking actual performance against targets with a Radial gauge chart.

Compact numbers: Automatically render high-volume numbers into clean, human-readable formats ($2.4M instead of $2,400,000) that stay readable across any screen size.

Sankey diagrams: Map multi-stage conversion funnels, user drop-offs, budget allocations, and material flows with native Sankey diagrams.

Mapping multi-stage conversion flows with a native Sankey diagram.

Drilling into multi-level nested data within a Hierarchical table.

Plotting frequency distributions and outliers across numeric variables with a Histogram.

Visualizing entity relationships, clusters, and bottlenecks with a Network chart.

Keep stakeholders engaged with a boardroom-ready design and faster, more focused interactivity:.

A modernized dashboard: More modern typography, refined spacing, cleaner table padding, and upgraded palettes give every dashboard a contemporary, polished look right out of the box.

Filters on visualizations (Preview): Apply and adjust filters directly on individual dashboard tiles, so viewers can isolate specific cuts of data without reloading the entire page.

Applying and adjusting chart-level filters directly on a modernized Looker dashboard tile.

Several of the new charts in this release started as custom visualization plugins in the Looker Marketplace. Because they are now supported natively in Looker, we are retiring the associated plugins from the Marketplace. Existing dashboards that use those Marketplace plugins will continue to work.

In a recent development, while Looker’s large native library covers most everyday analytics, every industry has specialized visualization requirements. A chipmaker may need to plot defect density across a silicon wafer map, a logistics team may want to overlay warehouse floor prepares onto live shipping metrics, and a finance team might ask for a multi-step variance bridge that follows internal accounting rules. These cases come up often. Previously, building one of these custom charts against Looker's Visualization API meant either writing JavaScript yourself or waiting for a front-end developer to help. Looker's agentic BI changes that.

In a recent development, to support these domain-specific builds, we are launching a new custom visualization skill in the open-source looker-skills repository. This skill lets you use your AI coding agent of choice, such as Antigravity, Claude or Codex, to develop, test, iterate, and deploy your own custom visualizations. Describe the chart in natural language, and the agent writes the code against Looker's Visualization API. You can refine the design conversationally until the chart looks right, and then have the agent deploy it for you.

Sunburst, KPI radar, and calendar heatmap charts generated with the Looker custom visualization skill.

It has been revealed that nobody on your team needs to know JavaScript. Still, if you prefer a specific JavaScript library, you can ask for D3, Vega-Lite, ECharts, Chart.js, or React, or have the agent draw the chart from scratch in SVG. Whatever approach you pick, the chart receives the underlying data from your LookML model and inherits native drill menus, cross-filtering, and dashboard controls alongside your standard tiles.

Industry observers note that this same visual system and agent-driven workflow also powers Looker Data Apps ( in preview). When your use case grows beyond a single custom chart tile into a multi-step operational workflow, you can use your AI agent to assemble a full data app that shares Looker's modernized typography, palettes, and governed LookML metrics. Whether you’re adding a bespoke chart to an existing dashboard or building a standalone application, every view stays consistent and grounded in the same semantic model.

Explore the fresh native visualizations and modernized dashboard controls in your Looker environment today, or visit the Looker documentation to learn more.

Try the custom visualization skill in your own Looker project by visiting the open-source looker-skills repository on GitHub.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (200 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (200 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22515v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.

Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (186 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22495v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.

For the third time in a row, Google Cloud is recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Application Development Platforms, positioned highest overall on the Ability to Execute axis.1.

These days, it’s very clear to us that organizations are looking for AI to handle actual day-to-day work, stay strictly within compliance guardrails, and deliver measurable ROI. In the last year, nearly 500 Google Cloud customers each processed more than one trillion tokens. And a lot of that volume came from heavily regulated sectors like global banking, healthcare, and telecommunications.

Our customers choose Gemini because it delivers an open enterprise platform built for this level of production scale, by:.

Unifying the agent experience across everyday workflows.

Providing unrestricted model choice without vendor lock-in.

Practicing cost discipline before bills spiral, not after.

Governing agents through a single, centralized control plane.

In October, we confirmed a unified Gemini experience. The same Gemini you collaborate with every day is now your enterprise agent to get real work done. Instead of navigating disconnected developer consoles, consumer tools, and workplace add-ons, Gemini meets work wherever it already happens – collaborating natively inside surfaces like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, internal chats, web, and mobile.

Industry observers note that you give Gemini high-level business objectives rather than step-by-step instructions, and it orchestrates the necessary tools, context, and coworker agents to deliver a finished result. As employees engage it, the agent retains persistent memory, understands your specific business language, and respects enterprise permissions across every device. When a team automates a complex procedure, they can package it into a shared skill, turning one group’s procedural knowledge into a capability anyone across the organization can use.

It has been revealed that that shared foundation is what transforms agent building from an isolated engineering backlog into an organization-wide capability. At Dojo, one of UK’s leading payment providers, non-technical teams used this exact environment to stand up over 600 custom agents in just two months:.

Industry observers note that “When you can use natural language, anyone from HR to sales can turn their unique business experience into a custom AI agent in minutes. In two months, we created over 600 agents. The majority were built by our frontline business teams right inside Gemini, leaving our developers to focus on more complex challenges.” – Robert Howes, Chief Technology Officer, Dojo.

Sources indicate that google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading frontier model families, from Google, Anthropic and OpenAI, on a unified enterprise platform – and across every surface, from developer tooling in Antigravity to everyday productivity in Gemini for web, mobile, and desktop. Through the model garden, organizations can access over 200 models, drawing down existing cloud commitments on a single invoice without having to negotiate separate contracts.

At the same time, we are deeply proud of the pace of innovation coming out of Google DeepMind. Over the past month alone, we’ve rolled out a full generation of specialized models: Gemini 4 Argon for strong performance across complex software engineering, law, finance, and cyber defense; Gemini 4 Carbon for frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows; and now Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence with speed and efficiency to everyday coding and agentic execution.

In a recent development, by treating models as a diversified portfolio, we give our customers the freedom to optimize for speed, precision, and cost across every task. For PayPal, this flexibility is central to their strategy:.

“We built a unified LLM stack. That meant we ran our open source models on top of our inferencing stack on GKE, and we ran our close-sourced models on top of the Gemini platform. Developers get choice – Claude, Gemini, Open Source – through one consistent governed access layer. That’s why we love the model garden.” — Srinivasan Manoharan, Director of AI/ML Platform, PayPal.

A recurring concern we hear from enterprise leaders is the unpredictability of AI billing. When teams start scaling agents, pay-as-you-go pricing can feel like an open tab with no ceiling. That is why we optimize cost across every layer of the stack – co-designing custom TPU silicon, cluster networking, and foundation models as a single system to drive down baseline costs.

According to recent reports, at the execution level, we give finance and engineering teams the right levers to innovate without risking their margins. Gemini dynamically matches every task to the most cost-effective model, handling high-volume tasks with efficient models, only escalating to frontier reasoning models for complex problem-solving. Paired with native FinOps controls – including project-level monthly spend caps, anomaly detection, and Flexible Savings Aims – leaders get hard financial boundaries and clear visibility.

For companies processing massive volumes of data, this approach makes all the difference. At Imgix, the engineering team prioritized this architectural discipline as they scaled visual processing:.

It has been revealed that “If we're using the most expensive model every single time, that's going to be a significant bill for our customers. So we use a cheaper model like Gemini Flash to figure out, ‘Does this image or video even need this AI feature?’ before routing further down the pipeline.” – Alfonso Acosta, Head of Engineering, Imgix.

In a recent development, when organizations empower employees to build and deploy agents at scale, governance cannot be an afterthought. It must be an inherent part of the environment in which those agents operate. With Gemini, every agent is assigned a dedicated Agent Identity, ensuring that all database queries, tool actions, and state transitions generate an auditable record tied directly to authorized roles. Execution occurs inside isolated runtime sandboxes, where Agent Gateway and Model Armor automatically scrub sensitive data, block policy violations, and enforce corporate compliance in real time.

That same control plane extends to how agents interact with corporate intelligence. Rather than requiring organizations to move, replicate, or duplicate sensitive records into yet another external repository, Gemini connects directly to live enterprise systems. Agents ground their reasoning in data across BigQuery, Cloud Storage, SAP, Salesforce, S3, and Azure – inheriting existing user access controls and keeping proprietary data strictly within its original perimeter.

Governed context and centralized control are what make tech giant-wide agent adoption possible. UKG relied on Gemini’s security, governance, and evaluation controls to skip building that foundation from scratch:.

Recent findings suggest that “The Gemini platform, it’s solving some of these key problems that we already were trying to solve — from hosting agents to securing them to the governance around them, evals to make sure they’re behaving correctly. Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (271 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward upcoming goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (223 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (223 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22482v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring fast and accurate delineation, such as surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural networks and Transformers, attaining high accuracy under limited computational resources remains difficult, because reducing model complexity often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context modeling, yielding an unfavorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. To address this, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that better balances local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes feature representations into low- and high-frequency components to extract multi-scale structural information, thereby mitigating detail loss during downsampling. We further develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational overhead. Evaluated on four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart) under both 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast inference. On Synapse, for instance, it attains a DSC of 76.57% with only 8.025M parameters and 241.72 FPS, confirming a favorable accuracy-efficiency balance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction with lightweight local-global feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/apple1986/levit_unet_pp.

MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22464v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

#8228. Tech Report: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (238 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (238 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22446v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an vital post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

#8225. Breaking: Eyes in the Revision? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (192 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Eyes in the Revision? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (192 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22438v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.

Encoding, Decodability, and Use: A Five-Layer Framework for Benchmark Measurement Audits with Evidence from UAV Intent Recognition

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (222 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22434v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Benchmark accuracy is routinely read as evidence that a model understands the construct the benchmark measures. We propose and instantiate on AeroIntent a five-layer framework that decomposes that reading into observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour. The framework separates encoding, decodability, and use as distinct levels. In the instantiation, the observation layer is unreliable on 7 of the 20 Drone programs and floors the direct visual correlate of radial velocity at a 0.26\% scale change. The representation layer exposes two task-designed RGB features with nominal signals. RAFT flow radial bias reaches $r=+0.257$ ($p=0.030$), and bounding-box optical-flow divergence reaches $r=+0.203$ ($p=0.029$). No multi-feature readout gives a fold-mean test correlation above the cluster minimum detectable effect (MDE), and the largest positive global out-of-sample correlation is $r=+0.080$. The decoding layer sets the MDE at $|r|=0.599$ at the multi-feature Bonferroni threshold ($\alpha=0.00714$, power 0.80), and the observed $r=+0.080$ has power 0.00. Two injection experiments establish the MDE's condition from both sides: aligned injections are detected at or above the simulated power, and orthogonal injections are not detected. The use layer finds accuracy consistent with program memory (program-identity 0.937/0.597/0.210) and multi-region static cues. The behaviour layer is consistent with accuracy not requiring a radial-velocity readout (appearance 0.6552 vs bounding-box trajectory 0.4080, cluster-level paired $\Delta=+0.2471$, $p=0.0132$).

#8220. Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (254 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22392v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Listwise LLM rerankers cannot reliably rank hundreds of documents in a single call, and rely on schedules to orchestrate their calls. Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each. When a group holds more of the top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls become required. We show that the way candidates are split matters where such a quota can bind, and that, in expected cuts, the best split there deals them round-robin by retriever rank, like cards. Although not conceptually new, dealing has remained unanalyzed. We prove that, under a simple retriever model, no split with equal quotas cuts fewer of the true top ten on average, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. DealRank, the simplest schedule our analysis allows, is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules over six LLMs, in two rounds. It is consistently 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than BlitzRank with concurrent first calls up to a thousand candidates. There, it needs three rounds and is eleven times faster than the sliding window. In existing schedules such as BlitzRank, dealing reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality. Random partitioning appears equivalent at a quota of four, as predicted, but ties results to the seed and trails by 1.3 nDCG@10 points at a quota of one over a dense retriever.

#8216. RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (216 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (216 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22382v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Leveraging Segmentation Representations for Efficient Classification: A Self-Configuring Framework Based on nnU-Net

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (198 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22380v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a self-configuring framework that extends the nnU-Net workflow to both segmentation and classification in 3D medical imaging. Building on nnU-Net's self-configuring method, the framework reuses representations learned by a segmentation model for image-level classification. Its encoder features and predicted segmentation probabilities are used by a lightweight classifier. Two information-sharing strategies are investigated. In the frozen-backbone branch, features are augmented with region-of-interest information, predicted foreground volume, and segmentation confidence. In the adaptation branch, the final encoder stage is partially fine-tuned for classification, with an auxiliary segmentation loss to preserve segmentation-related information. Additional five-fold experiments showed that more complex configurations did not consistently improve classification performance. On the public validation leaderboard, our selected framework achieved an Overall score of 0.8056. In the official FLARE 2026 Task 2 final evaluation, our framework ranked first overall, achieving the highest DSC, NSD, and AUROC across all four testing tasks, including two hidden testing tasks. Local inference measurements also remained below the challenge limits of $60 \mathrm{s}$ per case and $4 \mathrm{GB}$ GPU memory. These results demonstrate the practical value of reusing segmentation representations for classification while maintaining a simple and efficient framework.
